articles.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field. Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims. There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles.title: Missing Victims, Hidden Crimes: Improving Estimates of Honor Killings Using Missing Data Imputation
articles.abstract: Very little accurate data on the incidence and prevalence of honor killings exists. While some countries have made strides to identify and track cases on an ongoing basis, many countries either have no official statistics or rely on outdated data and imprecise methodologies. More accurate and up-to-date statistics are needed to better direct resources, identify cases and behaviors for study and intervention, and reduce biases. Unfortunately, measuring honor killings is methodologically difficult. However, while single lists of honor killings cannot accurately estimate the number of events, two or more lists in combination can, using multi-systems estimation (MSE). In this paper, we test the application of MSE to honor killings in four countries: Canada, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States by comparing estimates from MSE to counts of cases produced by aggregating multiple lists from each country. We find that MSE produces plausible estimates that demonstrate that even in seemingly complete lists of individuals or cases underestimate the scope of honor killings in these countries.

articles.title: Beyond Screen Time: Context, Valuation, and Self-Limitation of Mobile Phone Use
articles.abstract: Do people spend too much time on their phones? "Screen time" has come under scrutiny for its effects on health, cognition and sociability. In this paper, we conceptualize mobile phone use as a practice (Shove, 2003; Warde, 2005) and analyze how users evaluate and regulate their digital consumption. We draw on 45 in-depth semi-structured interviews with a diverse sample of French mobile phone users. We report three main findings. First, users’ accounts of their activity distinguish embedded activities and overflowing activities - that compete with other practices. Second, users' valuation of their digital activities depends not only on their nature (e.g. social media), but on their spatial and temporal context. Third, we identify four self-limitation strategies and show that context-based ones are the most effective. These results contribute to the debates on digital overconsumption, and the role of platform design in generating the practices they claim to help people reduce.

articles.title: Digital Preservation in Academic Libraries: The University of Ibadan Experience
articles.abstract: This study examines digital preservation practice at Kenneth Dike Library (KDL), University of Ibadan, to identify infrastructure, practices, challenges, and context sensitive strategies for sustainable stewardship in Nigerian academic libraries. Using a descriptive survey of the 15 library and ICT professionals directly involved in preservation activities, the research measures awareness, available infrastructure, preservation practices, major constraints, and preferred sustainability strategies. Results indicate uniformly high awareness and consensus that core preservation practices (digitisation, backups, metadata application, use of preservation tools, and integrity checks) are performed regularly. The library possesses essential digital repository infrastructure and technical support, but respondents identify poor internet connectivity, inadequate funding, and unreliable power as the most significant obstacles. Staff training, adoption of open source tools, inter institutional collaboration, hybrid storage approaches, and increased funding were unanimously recommended as sustainable strategies. Crucially, respondents strongly endorsed the need for locally adaptable, context sensitive preservation frameworks; however, opinions diverged on the adoption of specific low bandwidth or offline first technical designs. The study concludes that while KDL demonstrates strong knowledge and commitment to digital preservation, long term sustainability requires targeted investment, infrastructure resilience, capacity building, and policy formalisation—preferably through solutions adapted to the Nigerian technological context. Keywords – Digital Preservation, Academic Libraries, Nigeria, Digitisation, Repositories

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the New Science of Culture
articles.authors: Douglas Guilbeault, Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan, James Evans
articles.abstract: Cognition and culture have long been treated as parallel objects of study, joined more by metaphor than by mechanism. We argue they are co-constituted in a manner now empirically tractable: subjectivities can be measured as local trajectories through a high-dimensional cultural field, and the field is itself the aggregate of those trajectories. Recent advances in machine learning, including embedding methods and large generative models, provide the first general framework for measuring this co-constitution from micro-cognition to macro-social structure. Vector geometry recovers individual conceptual structure, organizational communication, and large-scale ideologies; captures multimodal cultural content beyond text; and generates testable predictions about cultural emergence, including the simultaneous arrival of independent discoveries across distant minds. We treat this predictability of simultaneous innovation as evidence for the co- constitutive view: when the geometry of the cultural field is measurable, trajectories of cognitive search through it become predictable. We then examine generative AI agents as simulators of human subjectivity and as a qualitatively new coordinating substrate whose insertion into social life introduces evolutionary dynamics unprecedented in human cultural history. We formalize this reflexive condition as a Heisenberg-like Uncertainty Principle for generative AI: as instruments for fixing a culture’s position grow more precise, our capacity to predict its trajectory degrades, because the machinery of cultural description and cultural action have merged. We close with ethical questions raised by AI-mediated cultural drift, recursive synthetic culture, and the limits of human cultural agency, offering guidelines for safe, equitable, and privacy-preserving research on AI and culture.

articles.title: Mapping Europe’s Digital Acquis. A Granular History of EU Digital Policymaking
articles.abstract: Over the last decade, digital policy has moved to the center of EU policymaking. Yet we have little systematic knowledge of how much of it the EU has produced, where it is made, or what it does. We map the EU's digital acquis from 1979 to today: we decompose every regulation, directive, and decision into nearly two million recitals and (sub-)articles and classify each with a two-stage pipeline that distills a human-validated ensemble of large language models into open encoder models. The share of digital provisions in newly adopted legislation rose from under one percent in the 1980s to roughly one in ten, and most sit outside the flagship digital acts. Testing two prominent claims, we show that digital legislation has become more assertive over time, with its obligations and prohibitions falling increasingly on private actors, and that it is more rights-oriented than the rest of EU law yet still more market- than rights-oriented, with the rights it invokes being mostly civil. We release our provision-level dataset, classification models, and a Python package for building granular legislative corpora: open infrastructure for measuring not just how much legislation there is, but what it says and does.

articles.title: From Getting Ahead to Staying Ahead: Reference Points and Repeated Investment in Status Maintenance
articles.abstract: As rapid technological change reshapes the skills employers demand and increases the importance of post-entry human capital accumulation, including reskilling, educational attainment no longer determines a person's position once and for all at labor-market entry. Research on stratification has nonetheless concentrated on who attains advantaged positions, and the repeated investment required to hold a position once attained remains underexplored. This study develops a model that extends the relative risk aversion hypothesis to an infinite-horizon setting, incorporating depreciating status and an endogenously updated reference point, to analyze the decision to invest in maintaining status. The results show that past success does not end the need for further learning: those who have reached higher positions face a larger reference-dependent loss and invest defensively even when resources and costs are identical. Moreover, I identify conditions under which more effective training widens rather than narrows status gaps, and show that individual credential renewals aggregate into a rising credential standard. Wider participation in adult learning is therefore compatible with a stable status order, and the locus of stratification may shift from who gets ahead to who can stay ahead.

articles.title: University-affiliated sustainability badges: Shared identity, tourist perceptions, and hotel manager receptivity
articles.authors: Peter Lewin, Danyelle Greene, Anna Kristina Zinn, Sarah MacInnes, Sara Dolnicar

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Hotel sustainability research shows that pro-environmental behaviour‑change interventions are often effective in field experiments, but widespread adoption by hotels remains limited. One possible explanation is that hotels lack external recognition that would make adopting these measures visible to guests and rewarding to managers. This study investigates whether university-affiliated sustainability badges could serve as a recognition mechanism, testing their effectiveness across two studies drawing on Signalling Theory and Social Identity Theory. In an online experiment (N=975), prospective hotel guests viewed simulated hotel booking pages featuring one of the four badge options, or no badge, across budget, mid-range, and luxury hotel pricing segments. All badge variations increased perceived hotel sustainability and guests’ sense of belonging to a community of environmentally conscious travellers (group identification). Badges did not trigger negative emotions, but the university affiliated logo did not perform better than a generic environmental logo on almost all measures, suggesting these effects are based on the presence of any badge, rather than the university partnership specifically. Semi-structured interviews with ten hotel managers found conditional receptivity to university-affiliated badges, primarily through a sense of shared values and community orientation with the partnering institution (collective values) rather than the badge’s function as a credibility signal. These findings suggest that collective values and shared identities, rather than signalling, may be the more promising mechanism for engaging hotels and guests around sustainability initiatives, and offer an encouraging direction for potential university-hotel partnerships that may translate into the future implementation of pro-environmental behaviour change interventions.

articles.title: Can Ethnic Divisions Explain Poor Economic Growth in Resource Rich Countries? The Case of the Middle East
articles.abstract: This paper addresses the question of the effects of ethnic diversity on economic growth. It extends the cross-country growth regressions in Easterly and Levine (1997) by allowing for growth effects of natural resources to depend on the amount of ethnic fractionalization to see if ethnic diversity, natural resource abundance, and the interaction of the two can explain Middle Eastern Countries' poor economic performance. And, the answer is found to be “yes”: The resource curse applies in ethnically heterogeneous countries but not in homogenous ones.

articles.title: Toward non-textual representation of social anthropology: Modeling cultures as knowledge graphs
articles.authors: Manolis Peponakis, Sarantos Kapidakis, Doerr, Martin, Tountasaki, Eirini
articles.abstract: The study examines the emerging field of knowledge representation in the context of the semantic web and linked data, with a focus on knowledge produced within the social sciences - particularly in sociocultural anthropology. It starts from the premise that natural language, especially its textualized form, has long been the primary vehicle for producing and communicating anthropological research. Informed by theoretical approaches from information science, the study explores how computational methods may offer alternative modes of structuring and representing anthropological knowledge. It challenges the dominance of text as the sole representational medium and highlights the potential of semantic modeling to open new epistemological pathways. At the same time, it acknowledges the conceptual and methodological challenges involved in such a transition. This approach shifts emphasis away from metrics and programming, foregrounding processes of conceptualization, semantics, meaning, and reasoning as key to engaging with anthropological knowledge in digital environments.

articles.title: The Protection Gap Nobody Is Closing: Litigation, Legal Fictions, and the Populations Climate Law Still Can't See
articles.abstract: Climate change has displaced hundreds of millions of people since 2008, and projections suggest this number could reach 216 million by 2050. Yet the legal architecture meant to respond to this displacement, from the 1951 Refugee Convention to more recent litigation and regional treaties, remains built around a single, hidden assumption: that the displaced person has already moved or has the capacity to move. This paper argues that legal visibility in climate migration tracks mobility capacity rather than hazard exposure, and mobility capacity in turn tracks wealth. Drawing on the Teitiota v. New Zealand and Daniel Billy v. Australia decisions before the UN Human Rights Committee, and on the Kampala Convention as a rare case of binding regional protection, the paper develops an asymmetry matrix that maps legal protection against event speed and mobility capacity. The gap is shown to be deepest for populations facing slow-onset degradation with low mobility capacity, such as Sahel herders and smallholders in Uganda and Zambia, who are simultaneously the most exposed and the least able to generate a legal claim. The paper concludes by proposing non-migratory policy channels, including vulnerability mapping, early warning systems, cash transfers, and planned relocation, as necessary complements to a legal framework that cannot reach the populations it is meant to protect.

articles.title: "Platform Popular Culture": Concept Initiative, Theoretical Construction and Case Analysis
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of an increasingly platformized online culture and new forms of youth-led cultural practice, this study proposes platform popular culture as a mid-range theoretical concept, aiming to move beyond both the "mainstream culture–subculture" binary and the "resistance–incorporation" paradigm long dominant in subcultural analysis. Drawing on youth subculture studies, popular culture studies, and platformization research, the study develops three analytical toolkits: (1) the "negotiation–mutual constitution" relationship between platform popular culture and mainstream culture; (2) a logic of production shaped by the user–platform–capital triad; and (3) the cultural function of interpreting social hotspots. Empirically, it examines two typical cases from Rednote—the "Love Your Old Self" self-care meme and citywalk—combining longitudinal data monitoring with BERTopic modeling to analyze the emergence, circulation, and practice of both value-oriented and practice-oriented forms of platform popular culture. The findings validate the concept's theoretical value and cultural function, clarify the strengths and limitations of the proposed framework, and contribute to a more systematic research agenda on youth online culture while offering a fresh vantage point for studying the platformization of cultural production.

articles.title: Tracking nature dependencies and nature-related risks: integrated environmental-economic accounting in Australia
articles.authors: Crystal Bradley, Sarah Taylor, Michael Vardon, Mitchell Lyons, Sarah Clement, Carl Obst

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Ecosystems and the services they provide underpin economic production and human wellbeing, yet these dependencies are poorly measured and rarely monitored. As a result, conventional economic statistics often fail to show how ecosystem decline may threaten production and wellbeing. The missing information can be supplied by the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA), an international statistical standard for tracking environmental stocks and flows, including ecosystems and their services, which is interoperable with the System of National Accounts (SNA). We assess how a linked system of SEEA and SNA accounts can be used to measure and track nature-economy dependencies, including the transmission of physical risk. We argue that accounting for ecosystem services provides the main connection between nature and the economy. The connection depends upon accounts using consistent classifications and typologies, which we call material join keys, so that information about ecosystems, ecosystem services, industries and economic activities can be reliably linked. Applying the approach to Australia, a gap analysis shows that existing ecosystem service accounts already track several of the dependencies most important and at risk from ecosystem decline, but only partially, and that priority new accounts for water and food security, health, climate resilience and supply chain resilience are needed to close the remaining gaps. Realising the potential of integrated accounting supports the mainstreaming of natural capital considerations into decision-making and public policy, and the proactive management of nature-related risks.

articles.title: Food Environment Policy Index for the German States: A structured policy analysis with expert consultations
articles.authors: Franziska Wiebke, Peter von Philipsborn, Anette E. Buyken

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Abstract Introduction Subnational governments can play an important role in influencing food environments, particularly in multilevel governance systems such as Germany, where multiple levels can introduce policy and legislation. Yet the extent to which subnational governments, including the German States, use this potential remains largely unexplored. To make the scope of subnational food environment policies explicit, comparable and assessable, we developed a state-specific Food Environment Policy Index (Food-EPI), using Germany as an example. Methods The INFORMAS Food-EPI served as the starting point for our analysis. To adapt it to the subnational level, we followed an iterative process drawing on four data sources: i) legal and policy documents and secondary sources; ii) key informant interviews; iii) written feedback from experts; and iv) an online expert workshop. Results The state-specific Food-EPI covers 25 indicators across 12 domains, outlining the substantial scope of subnational governments to influence food environments. The policy domains are food labelling, advertising and marketing, subsidies, provision, retail and food service and waste, combined with six infrastructure support domains. We drew on 128 documents to identify 57 good practice examples from subnational governments and adapted the INFORMAS protocol into a streamlined four-step approach. Conclusion We demonstrate that it is feasible to develop a tool to assess food environment policy at the subnational level, that systematically outlines the substantial influence of subnational governments on food environments. Applying the state-specific Food-EPI in practice to German States is an important next step to further corroborate its practical relevance.

articles.title: Beyond the Dark Figure: A Causal and Probabilistic Analysis of Crimes Against Women in India

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Most research on violence against women in India depends on administrative police records. However, this raw data often suffers from severe reporting biases and fails to account for massive population differences between districts. To address these flaws, this study applies causal inference, hierarchical modeling, and machine learning to better understand local crime dynamics. By combining two decades of National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) statistics with 2011 Census demographics, we map both the spatial distribution and the true sociological drivers of this violence. We found no evidence of geographic clustering; a Moran's I analysis shows the violence is distributed randomly across the country. Furthermore, our mixed-effects hierarchical models indicate that broad state-level policies explain less than 1% of the variance in local crime rates. Furthermore, by applying Pearl's do-calculus and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), we isolate the causal effects of the male-female literacy gap and urbanization, proving that urbanization is the dominant driver of reporting rates. A Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) correctly isolates the passage of the 2013 Criminal Law (Amendment) Act as an administrative reporting shock yielding an 88,879 annual case surge rather than a behavioral epidemic. Finally, Bayesian Belief Networks are utilized to model highly nonlinear sociological interactions, providing a mathematical framework for proactive risk assessment.

articles.title: The Economic Costs of Nepal's Open Border with India: A Case Study on Smuggling
articles.abstract: The border between Nepal and India, which was opened in 1950 by the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, has created unprecedented conditions for developing cultural and social ties between the countries. However, the open border has also led to severe negative consequences for the national economy of Nepal. This research aims to discuss the effects of smuggling through the 1,880 km border and analyse the situation in the context of the foreign trade deficit and the deteriorating economic situation in the country. Based on the data presented by the study, it is possible to draw the conclusion that smuggling contributes significantly to the trade deficit between Nepal and India. Smuggling of gold, drugs, agricultural products, and people constitutes a substantial part of trade between the countries. It is reported that 42.5% of the officially recorded trade between Nepal and India is smuggling, which results in a loss of 33.5 billion rupees for the Nepalese economy. In addition to the loss from unofficial trade, the state loses 3.58 billion rupees in duty and 3.71 billion rupees in value-added tax. The article also reports that the trade deficit in Nepal this year amounts to NPR 180 billion, of which a considerable part is caused by smuggling. Thus, the current situation in which Nepal allows free trade between the countries is extremely disadvantageous for the national economy. The study provides multiple examples that prove the severity of the problem, including the cases of Badhaiyatal and Bardibas, where the largest seizures of marijuana, gold, and peas in recent years were registered. According to official data, 30,000 people are trafficked illegally into Nepal every year, resulting in significant losses for the economy. The causes of the problem include the initial policy of open borders, insufficient control mechanisms, corruption, and taxation issues. However, the authors of the article believe that a smart border is necessary to ensure the prosperity of the Nepalese economy through trade with India.

articles.title: Zero FTE Does Not Mean Zero Work: Administrative Classification and the Political Economy of Academic Labor
articles.abstract: Universities often assign faculty appointments through percentages, salary lines, workload allocations, and other administrative categories. Yet a zero-FTE or unpaid appointment can still carry substantive expectations. This study examines that apparent contradiction as a problem of academic labor. Drawing on Marxian political economy, with selective guidance from Labour Process Theory, I conducted a critical analysis of eight publicly available university policy documents governing zero-FTE, dry, courtesy, affiliate, unpaid, and conflict-of-commitment arrangements. The documents were purposively selected because they explicitly paired zero or absent local compensation with language about contribution, duties, effort, institutional benefit, or professional obligation. Across the policies, three patterns recur. First, zero often describes a budgetary or appointment status rather than the absence of work. Second, the organizational beneficiary of academic labor need not be the unit that bears its salary cost. Third, unpaid activity can remain institutionally visible when universities need to regulate time, contribution, or commitment, even when the same activity creates no local salary obligation. The analysis does not imply that every unpaid affiliation is exploitative, nor does it treat every uncompensated activity as surplus-value production in a strict Marxian sense. Instead, it shows how administrative classification can separate labor from the obligations attached to labor. The central asymmetry is simple: institutions are often better at preventing double payment than at preventing double work. Zero FTE is an administrative category. It is not a description of human activity.

articles.title: Cities for Seasons - In favor of microclimate diversity as alternative to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours in competitively livable cities in temperate climates
articles.abstract: Temperate cities compete to rank the world’s most livable, while competing under the same premise: A summer period with relatively abundant life on the streets, and a winter period with relatively sparse life on the streets, owing to cold stress. Yet these cities – Copenhagen, London, New York, Melbourne, Paris, Vancouver, Vienna – have been implementing strategies that are directly detrimental to the elongation of their streets’ active seasons: Motivated by increasingly frequent and intense heat events, they have set out to mitigate urban heat island effects, aiming to eliminate any time that any surface exceeds the upper limit of the human thermal comfort range. But with no spatial or temporal limit to these strategies and guidelines – the approach is consistently the more heat island mitigation the better – these strategies inadvertently incentivize a complete, systematic prevention of warm microclimates that, while they may be too hot during the heat waves, can be highly attractive the rest of the year. Therefore this thesis employs a tri-seasonal rhythmanalysis to explore the dynamic use of places that are subject to urban heat island effects as well as of places which are subject to cooling effects. In the terminology of the author, these places together constitute an area with “high microclimate niche development”, which stands in contrast to the areas with low niche development that are predictably reproduced when focusing on UHI mitigation, and when optimizing according to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours. It finds that when the warm niches are accessible – like at south facing ‘soft edges’ of interactive buildings – they significantly extend the local active season: That in early spring, when people first move out of the buildings, they tend to gravitate toward the warm, south facing edges of these buildings, after which a spillover effect happens from these warm niches, into adjacent cooler niches, and back, throughout the days as well as the seasons, whereby the warm niches exhibit a pulsing, gravitational pull. This descriptive model is synthesized into a prescriptive model and a series of preliminary methods of analysis, which aim to display and thereby enable assessment of microclimate diversity, and of synergy with complementary parameters. As proof of concept, these models are used to formulate re-designs. This approach is found to synergize with contemporary approaches for flood mitigation and for biodiversity, but demands one key shift: acknowledging that, in temperate cities, heat islands can play a substantial positive role. It argues that this shift appears as the logical conclusion of the development started by Jan Gehl when he defended the import of the (at the time) uniquely Mediterranean café culture to ‘cold’ northern Europe. It predicts that this shift may transform urban life in temperate cities in a similarly profound way.

articles.title: kîkway itôtaman ôta Dante? The nine circles of community-engaged Indigenous research hell
articles.abstract: Research involving Indigenous Peoples has historically been harmful to Indigenous Peoples and their communities. In recent years, however, growing public awareness of Indigenous Peoples' experiences and histories through national and international initiatives has made research involving Indigenous Peoples much more equitable. However, in this renaissance of change, researchers who work with Indigenous communities and use community-engaged methodologies often rely on terms such as relational, co-designed, collaborative, and community-engaged. This reliance is not a reliable indicator that Indigenous communities themselves have meaningful authority over research that affects them and the knowledges they share. Because of this, I take a satirical, slightly humorous approach, drawing on Dante's Inferno and Neuroskeptic's Nine Circles of Scientific Hell to elucidate recurring issues in research involving Indigenous Peoples, more specifically research that uses, or seems to use, community-engaged methodologies. In the article, I conceptualize the nine circles while identifying problems that recur in community-engaged research involving Indigenous Peoples. These problems encompass tokenistic engagement, late or forced consultation, extractive relationships, pan-Indigenization, having Indigenous advisory bodies without decision-making power, checkbox approaches to Indigenous methodologies/frameworks, possessive relationships to data, poor knowledge return, and helicopter research. This article thus uses satire to make already existing contradictions around authority, accountability, governance, reciprocity, and relationships harder to ignore and to show that “relational” language is not enough, especially if Indigenous communities are not given meaningful authority to shape research projects involving themselves or their knowledges.

articles.title: ANTHROPOLOGY, COMPLEXITY AND THE LIMITS OF TOP-DOWN CONFLICT ANALYSIS
articles.abstract: Conflict analysis often approaches violence through externally defined categories, scales, and institutional frameworks that simplify complex social relations into identifiable problems and corresponding interventions. Similarly, contemporary localization paradigms seek to bring analysis, decision-making, and intervention closer to affected communities. Yet treating “the local” as a given and bounded site of action can obscure the relations of power through which local social worlds, conflicts, and capacities to act are themselves produced. The problem, I argue, is not only the use of externally defined categories to describe conflict, but also the analytical separation of the local from the wider relations through which it is constituted. Drawing on long-term ethnographic research among Rendille pastoralists in northern Kenya, I propose an approach that does not treat the community or conflict as a bounded system, but instead reconstructs how actors themselves distinguish forms of violence and the different forms of power through which they are produced and governed, including physical force, symbolic power, and control over information. The ethnographic case shows how resource disputes, ethnic conflict, livestock raiding, political competition, and cross-border processes constitute analytically distinct but increasingly interconnected domains as relationships among socially differentiated actors and their access to different forms of power change across scales. Changes in one domain can alter the conditions through which conflict is interpreted and governed in another, while broader political, economic, ecological, and geopolitical processes are incorporated into local relations and transformed through them. I argue that complexity emerges not from the simple interconnectedness of everything, or from the number of actors and factors involved, but from changing relationships among systems of order, forms of power, temporalities, and scales. The local is therefore not treated as a pre-existing scale, but as an empirical configuration produced through these relations. Methodologically, I propose an emic, participatory, and multiscalar approach in which ethnographic reconstruction precedes formal modeling. Complexity-science methods, including participatory mapping, System Dynamics, network analysis, and other quantitative approaches, can then formalize and investigate dynamics identified ethnographically, such as feedback, interdependence, emergence, and nonlinearity. This provides a methodological pathway from the emic to the systemic: beginning with local relations to reconstruct how power operates, how processes connect across scales and temporalities, and where change can actually occur.

articles.title: When is Forgetting an Advantage?: Considering Organizational Amnesia at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Organizational amnesia in the public sector is often understood as a pathology and source of capability loss. In response, literature is emerging framing the potential advantages of organizational amnesia; however, the nature and source of potential advantages remain under-developed. In this paper, I argue DARPA provides a counter-intuitive case of organizational design which structurally reinforces organizational amnesia while it is, seemingly paradoxically, perceived as reinforcing capacity for pursuing high-risk, high-reward research & development (R&D) programs. Taking a qualitative perspective, I argue DARPA has evolved an organizational structure which shapes how routinization proceeds, with downstream implications on dynamic capabilities. I frame this work as being driven by memory conditions, oriented around reduced memory formation, reduced memory availability, shaped willingness for memory recall, and shaped utility of memory recall. I pose DARPA as a unique case study in the organization of memory in public sector funding organizations.

articles.title: How Parties Reshaped Class Participation: The Central Role of Parental Abstention
articles.abstract: Labour’s programmatic realignment in the 1990s withdrew a generation of working-class adults from electoral politics. Abstention rose disproportionately in the working class, reshaping the formative environments of subsequent cohorts. This paper traces the lagged intergenerational effects of that shift on class inequalities in turnout. The analysis draws on linked parent-child data from the British Household Panel Survey and Understanding Society (1992-2025), in which parental class position and electoral participation are observed directly during respondents’ formative years, and combines random-effects panel models with parametric and nonparametric decomposition. The association between class origin and adult turnout is stable across cohorts socialised before and after realignment. What differs is the distribution of formative environments: exposure to parental abstention is substantially more unequal across class origins in the later cohort. Parental participation accounts for over forty per cent of the post-realignment class-origin gap, net of class destination and educational attainment, and counterfactual estimates suggest that equalising exposure would return the gap to pre-realignment levels. Class inequalities in turnout are therefore in part the lagged consequence of party strategy, transmitted through households and carried into the electorate by successive cohorts.

articles.title: How should VAWG be measured in the new UK strategy to halve it in ten years?
articles.abstract: New metrics to evaluate the UK government’s strategy to halve violence against women and girls in ten years are proposed. If the strategy to reduce violence against women and girls is to concern the whole of government and the whole of society, then its measurement needs to mainstreamed not confined to a separate silo. Three issues in building metrics are identified and resolved: strategic (mainstreaming rather than a separate silo), conceptual (defining ‘women and girls’ and extending violence to include non-domestic; distinguishing between different forms of ‘violence’); and technical (strengths and weaknesses of different data sources and statistical techniques). While the new government headline metric of a combined measure using a single data source has problems. Modifying the combined metric and adding five supporting metrics and two additional data sources would address these, achieving compatibility with the main statistical series on violent crime, making visible the scale of the gender gap in more serious forms of violence, such as homicide, rape, and high frequency victims, and making visible specific forms particularly relevant to Black, minoritised and migrant women. This contribution to the indicators in the UK Strategy engages global debates while focusing on the English context with its specific epistemic systems that engage policy and data.

articles.title: Geographic Diversity and the Strategic Placement of Immigrant Candidates
articles.abstract: Immigrant-background populations remain underrepresented in national legislatures. A common explanation is that parties perceive immigrant-background candidates as electorally costly and therefore place them disproportionately in unwinnable contests. Existing research, however, pays little attention to the geographic concentration of immigrant-background populations, which can create electoral incentives as well as risks. We argue that parties strategically nominate immigrant-background candidates where demographic diversity generates electoral opportunity. Using original data on all candidates in German federal elections from 2002 to 2025, we show that immigrant-background candidates are more likely to be nominated in districts with larger immigrant populations, especially where those districts are electorally competitive. We further show that these nomination patterns can translate into electoral gains, but the effect is limited. The strongest evidence comes from Turkish co-ethnic dynamics, and the electoral benefits are concentrated in the Social Democratic Party, which has historically had the closest ties to Turkish-background voters in Germany.

articles.title: “TikTok refugees”: Motivations and political correlates of international platform migration
articles.abstract: This study investigates the motivations and political correlates of large-scale platform migration in a transnational context. While prior research has emphasized social and technological drivers, the political significance of migration remains underexplored. Building on theories of alternative political expression, political and media trust, and political efficacy, this study conceptualizes platform migration as an alternative political expression. Using an online survey of a group of users with sustained adoption of RedNote, we analyze the case of “TikTok refugees,” examining five motivational mechanisms – social influence, platform-use orientation, political expression, cultural openness, and collective identity frames – and a series of political characteristics with migration. The results show that lower political and media trust, lower external efficacy, and higher internal efficacy are significantly associated with affective and perceptual dimensions of migration. In addition, political expression and cultural openness emerge as the strongest motivators, while well-recognized motivations of social influence and platform-use orientation do not show statistically significant correlation. Taken together, the findings highlight platform migration as a complex, multidimensional behavior situated at the intersection of technological change and (geo)political dynamics.

articles.title: Converging Across Generations? Intergenerational Integration into Associational Life
articles.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen, Anders Bastrup Jørgensen, Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles.abstract: This article examines the extent to which immigrant-native gaps in voluntary association involvement, a key dimension of associational life, narrow across generations. Neo-assimilation theory suggests broad intergenerational progression, whereas segmented assimilation theory points to more heterogeneous trajectories across groups with different civic and religious backgrounds. To test these expectations, we examine intergenerational differences in voluntary association membership, active participation, and volunteering among non-Western immigrant-origin adults aged 18-50, using linked survey and register data from the Danish Citizenship Survey (N = 4,273). Logistic regression analyses reveal substantial intergenerational progression toward native levels of involvement. While first-generation immigrants are markedly less involved than natives, childhood immigrants and second-generation immigrants display involvement levels substantially closer to, and in some cases indistinguishable from, those of natives. Progression occurs broadly across groups with different civic and religious backgrounds, and groups with more distant backgrounds do not consistently exhibit less progression. KHB decomposition analyses further reveal that socioeconomic attainment and, especially, citizenship status account for substantial shares of the observed intergenerational progression, ranging from 40-47% for membership to 80-86% for volunteering. Overall, the findings extend neo-assimilation theory’s expectation of broad intergenerational progression to associational life and highlight the importance of structural and formal incorporation in this process.

articles.title: Double Adaptation: Negotiating Closeness and Managing Boundaries in Journalist–Politician Relations
articles.authors: Marina Urbanikova, Lenka Waschkova Cisarova, Iveta Jansová, Melanie Haberl, Folker Hanusch, Sophie Lecheler
articles.abstract: Closeness with politicians is both a professional resource and a potential risk for journalists, as it enables access to information but may compromise autonomy and integrity, particularly within today’s hybrid media environment. This study proposes the conceptual framework of double adaptation as a sensitizing, process-oriented lens for a more systematic understanding of how journalists manage boundaries with politicians, drawing on 96 semi-structured interviews with political journalists in Austria and Czechia. Double adaptation captures the dual process through which journalists adjust their practices in response to both immediate situational demands and structural conditions. Boundaries in journalist–politician interactions emerge through situational adaptation to specific contexts, requiring a careful balancing across multiple dimensions of closeness. The analysis identifies nine such dimensions, grouped into two domains: interactions and relationships. The study further identifies individual factors shaping situational adaptation, including symbolic and pragmatic approaches to boundary management, and situational factors such as personal affinity. Simultaneously, boundaries result from structural adaptation operating at organizational, professional, and systemic levels, influenced by digital transformation, economic pressures, and the professionalization of political communication. Together, these insights advance a more systematic and processual conceptualization of boundary management in political journalism by linking everyday interactional practices to broader structural transformations.

articles.title: The Writing on the Wall: Foreign Coup Success and Preemptive Purges in Autocracies
articles.abstract: There is broad scholarly consensus that leaders' perceived vulnerability to removal through coups determines when they act to weaken regime elites' capacity to organize a coup. Existing research, however, primarily examines domestic sources of leaders' perceptions of coup threats and overlooks the influence of foreign events. This study contends that successful foreign coups within the same region increase leaders' perceived vulnerability to coup threats, prompting preemptive purges of potentially threatening regime elites before such threats materialize domestically. We test this argument using novel monthly data on elite purges in autocracies from 1980 to 2010. By leveraging plausibly exogenous variation in foreign coup outcomes and a difference-in-differences approach, we demonstrate that foreign coup success increases the likelihood of authoritarian purges. These findings underscore the important yet frequently neglected role of foreign events in prompting autocrats to shift the leader-elite power balance in their favor.

articles.title: A Royal Effect: The Impact of Princess Leonor of Spain’s University Choice on Admission Outcomes
articles.abstract: In April 2026, Princess Leonor, heir to the Spanish throne, announced that she would begin a degree in Political Science at Carlos III University of Madrid (UC3M) in the forthcoming academic year. Since the announcement occurred nearly two months before students submitted their university admission applications, the Princess’s choice may have affected admission outcomes in three ways: by shifting preferences toward Political Science across universities, enhancing the attractiveness of UC3M across degree programs, or increasing demand for Political Science at UC3M over and above these two effects. Using public data on admission cutoff scores over an 11-year period and a difference-in-differences-in-differences model, I observe no general effect on Political Science across universities or on UC3M across degree programs. However, I do find a large and statistically significant impact of the Princess’ announcement on the admission cutoff score for Political Science at UC3M. The results emphasize how consequential the behavior of influential people might be, while also highlighting the volatility of decisions about university enrollment.

articles.title: You cannot decompose injustice: interaction, intersection, random effects and simple means in the evolution of MAIHDA
articles.abstract: Random effects intersectional analysis has promoted the multidimensional study of health inequalities, and the intersectional application of Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) is increasingly used to describe them. Its usual implementation fits an empty random effects model followed by a model adjusting for the variables that define the strata, and reads the remaining between-stratum variance as the intersectional effect. In this essay I trace how that convention grew, including my own contribution to it, and explain why my opinion has changed. Intersectionality, as originally formulated, is not about statistical interaction. The expression "more than the sum of its parts" refers to the uniqueness of a social position, not to an arithmetic operation. Intersectional strata are indivisible analytical units. I propose the term intact strata for strata kept whole in the analysis. I recall that random effects shrinkage describes a modelled population rather than the observed one, and present Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA) as the canonical design for the framework. Each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and the three MAIHDA components, specific contextual effects (SCE), general contextual effects (GCE) and discriminatory accuracy (DA), are obtained on the probability scale. Keeping strata intact does not banish interaction. It relocates it, as effect modification between the intact stratum and the structural axes, such as geography, time or institution, along which the position is lived. You cannot decompose injustice. You can describe it whole, and you can measure what the structures around it do to it.

articles.title: LLM measurements that agree with human coders overall can still distort specific effects
articles.authors: Alexander K. Moore, Bingqing Li, Shane Wang, Matt Thomson
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in the social sciences as surrogates for human coders. Standard practice validates them by their correspondence with human measurements of the same stimuli using statistics like correlation. However, overall correspondence can conceal biases that distort specific claims. We demonstrate this with open-weight LLM ratings of 568 food and 1,811 scene photographs. Ratings inflate, attenuate, or reverse effects, and improving overall correspondence with prompts can improve one contrast while worsening another. Rankings also elevate some categories and demote others beyond what random errors of the same size typically produce. Across six prompts, some of these errors are shared, so sampling across prompts may continue to mask biases. We propose validating LLM coders against specific claims they will test rather than the general coding task.

articles.title: Cross-Validation as a Bandwidth Criterion for Geographically Weighted PCA: An Ethics of Ambiguity
articles.abstract: Geographically weighted principal component analysis (GWPCA) summarizes spatial multivariate structure through local eigen decompositions whose output depends strongly on a bandwidth, conventionally chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation (CV). While locating the bandwidth that minimizes CV, several competing minima are frequently observed. We focus on the implications of multiple ambiguous minima as the object of study. We formalize it through the CV-equivalent set ($H_{\mathrm{CV}}$) of bandwidths that the data do not distinguish from the CV minimum ($h_{CV}$) and show that bandwidths within this set differ materially in their bias--variance composition and loading structure. Simulations across eight data-generating processes show that wherever the covariance subspace varied locally, the equivalent set spanned roughly a quarter of the candidate range grid, and the oracle bandwidth typically lay inside the set while differing from $h_{CV}$. In applications to the Dublin voter turnout and the Kola geochemical survey, the same ambiguity appeared, and within-set disagreement between local loadings concentrated where the local eigengap was small. We offer these findings as the first in-depth study of the characteristics of CV as used in GWPCA, and recommend reporting standards to include the equivalent set, and mapping the local eigengap.

articles.title: "I don’t trust it, but I have to trust it": Trust vs Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK
articles.authors: Emma Palmer-Cooper, Emma Gentry, Elena Nichele, Mohammad Naiseh, Liz Dowthwaite, Tayyaba Azim, Mohamad Armouch, Frances Greenway, Mark Weal, Ann-Marie Hughes
articles.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can in-fluence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: 8 with lived experi-ence of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of de-veloper trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare pro-viders and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

articles.title: Brain drain outweighs brain circulation between the Global North and South
articles.authors: Andrew Herman, Jens Peter Andersen, Mathias W. Nielsen
articles.abstract: International research mobility is increasing, as is the expectation that high- and low-income countries will mutually benefit. The once-dominant view of research mobility as “brain drain” has been replaced by a more optimistic narrative of “brain circulation”, built on the idea of cyclical talent flows that advantage all countries involved. But does this brain circulation model reflect the full picture for low- and middle-income countries, whose development depends on producing and retaining scientific talent? Our analysis of 16 years of international mobility flows in science suggests otherwise. While brain circulation increasingly occurs through temporary positions, joint affiliations, and return migration, a persistent pattern of brain drain remains, with Global South countries losing a growing share of their best-performing scientists to the Global North. Moreover, a differentiated hierarchy of talent flows is visible within the Global South. Some of the countries that lose the most talent to the Global North also attract the most talent from other Global South nations, offsetting their losses. But many others see substantial outflows of local talent to both the Global North and other Global South regions, compounding the issue. This differentiated pattern is also visible in the multiplex network structure of national inflows and outflows, where the relationship between sending talent to the Global North and receiving talent from the Global South is weaker than one would expect in random networks with a similar structure. Overall, our findings suggest a mixed reality. While visiting and return migration likely produce mutual benefits for Global North and Global South countries alike, this talent circulation is unlikely to offset the Global South's direct and indirect loss of its best-performing scientists.

articles.title: Соотношение финансового и реального секторов как драйверов развития экономики: систематизация теоретических моделей в рамках 9-слойной схемы системы разделения труда // The Relationship between the Financial and Real Sectors as Drivers of Economic Development: Systematization of Theoretical Models within a Nine-Layer Scheme of the Division of Labor
articles.abstract: This meta-research is devoted to the systematization and conceptual comparison of key economic concepts that consider either the real sector and technological innovation, the financial sector, or state institutions as the fundamental drivers of economic development. Comparing traditional models is complicated by the fact that most authors focus on individual factors, ignoring complex interrelated relationships. To overcome this limitation, nine-layer scheme of the division of labor of Petr Shchedrovitsky is used as an integrative analytical framework, encompassing levels from natural resources and production technologies to knowledge accumulation institutions and monetary systems. The study spatially visualizes the theoretical perspectives of Karl Marx, R. Hilferding, V. Lenin, J. Keynes, H. Minsky, J. Schumpeter, and C. Perez, as well as those of Latin American structuralism, Japanese "knowledge capitalism," and the Chinese school of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Positioning these concepts on a single map allows us to demonstrate their mutual complementarity at different phases of technological and financial cycles and lay the foundations for the synthesis of a comprehensive socioeconomic theory. The study also identified four main phases of technological and economic cycles, during each of which the role of the financial sector shifts from stimulating to destructive. It is shown that state and national-institutional mechanisms (the Chinese model, the Japanese J-firm) are capable of blocking the speculative separation of the ninth layer from the real sector.

articles.title: Representation Without Power: Far Right Electoral Success and Violence in Weimar Germany
articles.authors: Felix Haass, Alexander De Juan, Daniel Bischof, Henry Thomson
articles.abstract: Far right parties often win elections without gaining access to power. Do such outcomes pacify extremist movements, or can they fuel violence? We study this question in Weimar Germany after the July 1932 Reichstag election, when the Nazi Party became the largest parliamentary force but remained outside government. We digitize Nazi candidate lists and Prussian police records on street violence, linking riots to candidates' home towns. Using a regression discontinuity design around district list cutoffs, we compare towns whose Nazi candidates narrowly entered parliament with towns whose candidates narrowly missed. Post-election Nazi-communist violence was substantially higher in towns represented by elected Nazi MPs, while no discontinuity appears before the election. Mechanism evidence from perpetrator coding, stormtrooper mood reports, and membership records suggests that representation without power redirected frustration toward the movement's violent wing. The findings show that electoral representation can intensify anti-democratic violence when far right parties win mandates but remain excluded from power.

articles.title: The China Mirror Learning through Difference in the Digital Age

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Under conditions of rapidly increasing societal complexity, understanding other civilizations might become an epistemological necessity for fostering adaptive capacities. Drawing on Weber's Verstehen, Jullien's method of the écart, Luhmann's theory of observation, and Koselleck's conceptual history, we propose a method of differential displacement to compare not simply different situations, but their dynamics, with the aim of exposing implicit assumptions. As a case study, following Jullien, we examine what the categories through which China approaches the digital transformation can reveal to Europeans about its purposes and governance. The goal is neither to endorse nor to criticize China, but to move beyond the simplistic duality of democracy and authoritarianism and examine what the difference reveals about Europe's own categories. We further argue that persistent misunderstanding of others can progressively feed a misunderstanding of one's own transformation. Under conditions of complexity surge, comparison can become a mechanism of collective intelligence and adaptive learning.

articles.title: Disaggregating the AI elite: Gender, age, and education differences among professionals engaged in AI development
articles.abstract: Amid the society-wide onrush of artificial intelligence, asking ‘who creates AI?’ holds great urgency. A questionnaire-based study conceptualising ‘AI elite’ as a narrower group than the conventionally considered ‘coding elite’ found that only 5% of the 16,808 engineering and technology professionals surveyed contributed significantly to their organisation’s projects for AI development, design, or deployment, with an additional 15% contributing somewhat. Examining predictors of AI-elite membership, path analysis revealed organisation position to be the strongest, suggesting a Matthew-effect pattern wherein pre-existing power informs control over AI. Gender shapes membership directly and indirectly (through education choices and access to senior positions), compounding women’s under-representation. Education likewise manifests both direct and mediated positive effects. Counter to expectations, variety in one’s everyday application of AI tools correlated negatively with participation in AI development. This evidence that the AI elite reproduces structural inequalities spotlights ramifications that warrant further research and well-targeted diversification efforts.

articles.title: The chilean health model in the context of latin america. 40 years of economic crises, spending policies and reforms
articles.abstract: This chapter analyzes the relationship between economic crises and health reforms in Latin America, with an in-depth focus on the Chilean case, from the origins of its health model to the present day, including a reflection on its possible future developments. The Chilean health model, as it is known today, was designed amid the international crises of 1975 and 1982 and the political crisis of the dictatorship, and it was consolidated during the economic growth of the 1990s. Its most significant reform, developed following the Asian crisis of 1997, resulted in the AUGE Plan, adopted in 2005, which increased access to a defined set of health conditions without changing the model's underlying structure. The 2008 global financial crisis, and later the 2019 social crisis, opened a new stage of debate over structural change, in which the segmentation between the public insurer (FONASA) and the private insurers (ISAPRES) has come to be seen as the central obstacle to an equitable and solidarity-based health system. The regional analysis shows that this relationship between crises and reforms is not unique to Chile, but follows a broader Latin American pattern, moving from market-oriented reforms in the 1980s and 1990s toward a growing consensus, strengthened by the COVID-19 pandemic, in favor of universal, solidarity-based public health systems.

articles.title: One meal, not the next: a two-day RCT testing effects of increased plant-based availability on direct and later food choice
articles.authors: Lotte de Lint, Wilhelmina Elisabeth Adriana Metje van Rookhuijzen, Rachelle de Vries, Emely de Vet
articles.abstract: Replacing animal-sourced foods with plant-based alternatives benefits the environment, animal welfare, and public health. Nudges have been found to promote plant-based selection in the moment, but whether they influence later, non-targeted behaviors remains underexplored. Effects on non-targeted behavior could make interventions more effective if they promote consistency in later plant-based choice, or less effective if they trigger compensatory animal-based choice. In a two-day randomized controlled trial (n = 200), we evaluated a Nudge plus intervention delivered on day 1. The intervention combined an increased availability of plant-based to meat sandwich varieties (3:1 vs. 1:3) with a post-choice identity cue informing plant-based choosers that their choice signaled they care about the environment. We assessed intervention effects on targeted behavior (day-1 plant-based lunch choice) and non-targeted behavior (day-2 plant-based lunch choice and 24-hour animal product consumption). Furthermore, we tested whether such effects were mediated by environmental self-identity or moderated by plant-based eating motivation. The increased availability tripled targeted plant-based choice, from 22% in the Reference condition to 66% in the Intervention condition. We detected no main effects of the intervention on either non-targeted outcome, with equivalence tests indicating a negligible effect on 24-hour animal product consumption. There was no evidence of mediation via environmental self-identity or moderation by plant-based eating motivation. Increasing plant-based availability produced a large immediate positive effect on plant-based choice, while the Nudge plus produced no detectable compensatory shifts in non-targeted behavior. These findings support increasing the relative availability of appealing plant-based over meat-based options in food service settings.

articles.title: Peace or Push? Understanding Global Patterns of Refugee Return
articles.abstract: Return is the main way refugee crises end, yet there have been few cross-national studies of when it actually occurs. A central expectation of the refugee regime is that refugees remain abroad while home is unsafe and return as security improves. Yet using a novel global dataset, I show that most returns occur during ongoing conflict, while many refugees remain abroad long after wars end. To explain these patterns, I argue that asylum countries and international organizations play major and underrecognized roles in shaping return, largely overlooked by existing micro-level research focused on refugees’ concerns about security at home. Return is substantially higher when refugees face exclusion policies or conflict in asylum countries, and when donor-funded UNHCR assistance lowers the costs of return. I introduce the Global Refugee Return Dataset, covering 293 origin--asylum dyads from 1980 to 2023, which documents returns systematically undercounted by UNHCR and provides new global data on de facto refugee conditions and UNHCR financing.

articles.title: Dangers of non-objective constructions and interpretations of history: Important assertions and takeaways from an Indian context
articles.abstract: This short and very brief paper in a way extends our previous papers and publications on historiography, though it is in many ways quite important to our core mission. Its importance cannot also not be discounted based on our general observation that non-objective and non-purposeful constructs of history are widely prevalent across the intellectual spectrum, and both from the left and the right, and various errors of omission and commission to this effect and deeply and foundationally entrenched. Therefore, it goes without saying that course-corrections are in order, and that the dangers of non objective and highly biased and prejudiced constructs of history, especially those driven and propelled by ideology must be driven home to the broader and larger public. These assume added importance and significance in the Indian context for several reasons. Firstly, it precludes a scientific temper being inculcated among the laity, as they cannot trust mainstream scholarship any longer. Scientific constructs of history are also so important to relegate religion to the background eventually, and keep it in its place. Such constructs also lead to a culture of non-objectivity becoming deeply entrenched and it invariably begets counter-reactions from other ideologically driven groups. In addition, it is bound to severely compromise interdisciplinary approaches and integration across multiple periods and geographies all of which are so essential to the healthy growth of scholarship. In situations and circumstances where there are ideologically-driven ding dong battles as is presently the case, we may even need to adopt an outside in approach and educate the general public about non-objective and non-scientific constructs of history first. We are also at a loss to understand why a culture of service of historians to science, society, and the education system is not well-entrenched, and immediate course corrections are in order to promote objectivity in mindset at all costs, and under all circumstances.

articles.title: Who Sees Politics in Sports? Norm Endorsement and Partisan Judgments from the 2026 World Cup
articles.authors: Morgan Wack, Daniel Vogler, Manuel Arrigo, Christian Pipal, Lucas Paulo da Silva
articles.abstract: Most Americans say politics should stay out of sports. Yet whether this norm is truly binding depends on whether people apply it when their own side violates the norm. To test this "apolitical sports" norm, we fielded a two-wave matched panel survey around the 2026 FIFA World Cup (N1=988; N2=699). During the tournament, U.S. President Donald Trump called FIFA to have an American player's red-card suspension lifted. We asked respondents to judge the incident directly and to judge a message on players' shirts, varied to support or protest a contentious U.S. policy. Overall, endorsing the norm predicted lower tolerance for political expression in sports, within each party separately, with a smaller own-side advantage. Following this widely reported violation, Democrats raised their endorsement while Republicans did not. What divided partisans most was what they counted as a violation, with Republicans reporting less political interference. In short, while both sides agreed with the norm, they disagreed about whether it had been broken. Our findings suggest that partisan accommodation can influence how citizens recall and conceive of potentially norm-violating events.

articles.title: Can volunteering substitute for paid work? Unemployment, volunteering, and life satisfaction across the life course
articles.authors: Arjen de Wit, Heng Qu, Rene Bekkers, Bianca Suanet
articles.abstract: Unemployment is consistently associated with decreased well-being, but other productive roles may partly compensate for the social and psychological resources lost through job loss. Using a mega-analysis on six longitudinal panel studies covering over 500,000 observations across 20 European countries, we examine how age and volunteer status moderate associations between unemployment and life satisfaction. First-difference models show that transitions into unemployment are associated with declines in life satisfaction, with stronger negative effects observed among younger and middle-aged adults than among older adults. Contrary to expectations, volunteering does not consistently buffer the negative association between unemployment and life satisfaction, although supplementary analyses indicate that the compensatory role of volunteering may vary across age groups and national contexts. These findings indicate that volunteering is not a universal substitute for paid work and that the capacity of alternative productive roles to maintain well-being following job loss depends on broader social and institutional conditions.

articles.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM). It draws on in-depth qualitative interviews conducted with 11 medical professionals between March 2024 and August 2025, as part of a broader study of genital self-image, motivations for FGCS, and clinical responses. FGM is criminalised in both countries, whereas FGCS is not, even though some procedures classified as FGCS technically fall within the legal and policy definitions of FGM. In 2008, professional societies in the Netherlands attempted to clarify the distinction but ultimately failed to establish concrete criteria, relying instead on what they regarded as a self-evident difference. Healthcare professionals are therefore left to interpret and navigate this boundary in practice, drawing on their own professional knowledge, moral reasoning, and sociocultural understandings. This ambiguity raises important questions about how medical professionals distinguish between FGM and FGCS in their everyday practice. Do they regard the two as fundamentally different, or do they recognise areas of overlap, and on what grounds? What forms of reasoning, knowledge, and professional or cultural frameworks inform their distinctions? To what extent do their views reflect, reproduce, or resist broader social, cultural, and political discourses?

articles.title: Service Colonisation of the Public Health Model of Bereavement Support: A Critical Review and a Refined Model
articles.authors: Yong Hao Ng, Bruce Rumbold, Torsten Schwalbach, Samar Aoun
articles.abstract: The public health model of bereavement support, introduced in 2012, proposed a tiered framework that emphasised community networks’ contributions, informal resources, and shared responsibility across sectors in addition to professional clinical intervention. This study systematically examines how the model has been taken up in the research literature through a combined deductive content analysis and Foucauldian-informed discourse analysis of 252 peer-reviewed articles that cite the model’s foundational papers. The deductive analysis reveals that individually oriented and clinically focused components, particularly triage, epidemiology, and risk factors, dominate the corpus, while community resources and resource allocation remain peripheral. The discourse analysis identifies three interconnected discursive formations: an over-psychologisation that evaluates bereavement as psychiatric risk; an over-professionalisation that positions health professionals as central authorities and renders communities subordinate; and a governmental logic that treats risks, needs, and support as fixed, individually centred categories. Together, these formations constitute what we term service colonisation, in which the institutional norms of the health sciences reshape a broad social framework into a tool for organising clinical resource distribution. This narrowing has material consequences for which services are funded, which populations are recognised as needing support, and whose knowledge is privileged in the design of responses. We propose a refined model that reframes need beyond clinical risk, repositions communities as constitutive agents rather than passive resources, introduces dynamism into the tiered structures, and foregrounds social and structural determinants of bereavement. These findings have implications for how bereavement support is conceptualised, researched, and organised across health and social care systems.

articles.title: Drivers of household electricity demand in highly electrified markets
articles.authors: Reza Serati, Anna Kristina Zinn, Siamak Layeghy, Bettina Grün, Marius Portmann, Sara Dolnicar

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: As the world transitions to renewable energies, the structure of national electricity markets will change. Queensland (Australia) is a pioneer market; it is one of the most highly electrified markets internationally. This study analyses drivers of household grid electricity imports using operational smart-meter data from 1,119,389 households and two linked surveys. Solar and battery ownership, dwelling type, household size, pool and electric-vehicle ownership, and climate zone are key drivers. Having a solar system, living in a unit and in smaller households is associated with lower electricity imports. Larger households with a pool and electric vehicles import more electricity. We discuss these findings in the context of previous studies of drivers of household electricity use conducted in more traditional power markets. By distinguishing grid imports from total household consumption, we show how distributed generation and storage reshape network demand and provide new evidence for forecasting and planning in highly electrified markets.

articles.title: Benefit conditionality, sanction rules and the self-rated health of the unemployed: a longitudinal analysis of European countries
articles.abstract: Background The health effects of unemployment vary across European countries. This study examines whether cross-country differences in behavioural conditionality - such as job-search requirements, availability requirements and statutory strictness of sanctions rules - may shape these health effects, and which aspects of conditionality matter most. Methods We combined panel data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC, 2014–2019) with OECD indicators on activation policy strictness in 30 countries. Using first-difference regression models, we estimated the effect of becoming unemployed on changes in self-rated health (five-point scale) and tested whether this effect was moderated by the strictness of each policy dimension. We controlled for individual-level and macroeconomic variables. Results Becoming unemployed was linked to a small but significant decline in self-rated health (−0.05, 95% CI[−0.06, −0.04]). This decline was steeper in countries with stricter statutory sanction rules (interaction = −0.04 [−0.08, −0.004]), ranging from −0.053 [−0.098, −0.017] in low-sanction countries to −0.105 [−0.135, −0.078] in high-sanction countries. Job-search and availability requirements showed no significant moderation. Interpretation Stricter statutory sanction rules are associated with worse self-rated health among job seekers. Reducing reliance on sanctions and ensuring supportive activation systems could help protect health during unemployment.

articles.title: Mapping disability inclusion in Canadian park employment: A scoping review of academic and organizational evidence
articles.authors: Hannah Dudney, Zeyad Ghulam, Tilak Dutta
articles.abstract: Objective: The objective of this scoping review is to map how disability inclusion and accessibility are considered in Canadian park employment literature and organizational discourse. The review will identify and summarize both peer-reviewed literature and organizational evidence to examine how workplace accessibility and disability inclusion are addressed in these settings, and the extent to which they are absent. Introduction: Parks and protected areas in Canada are key public-facing service environments that increasingly emphasize accessibility and inclusion in relation to visitor experiences. However, less is known about how these organizations approach employment inclusion for people with disabilities, across both academic literature and organizational documents. Inclusion criteria: This review will include sources that concern employment-related stakeholders such as employers, employees, managers or other decision-makers (Population). Literature, policies, and other organizational discourse will be examined to determine the extent they consider disability, accessibility, and disability-inclusive employment (Concept).
